panels.bubble_text: Theory was beautiful. Then the world caught fire.
panels.speaker: RADAR

panels.text: Last time, we watched a young mathematician imagine the simplest possible computing machine. Tape. Head. Rules. Beautiful. Elegant. Completely imaginary. Nobody had built one. Nobody needed to.

And then the world caught fire.

In 1936, Alan Turing's machine existed only on paper — a thought experiment. It was not designed to be built. But between 1939 and 1945, the Second World War created problems that no human mind could solve fast enough. Encrypted messages. Artillery tables. The atomic bomb. Theory had a deadline.

panels.prompt: A dark wartime operations room in the 1940s, maps pinned to walls, radio equipment crackling, urgent officers leaning over tables covered in coded messages and calculations, dim yellow lamp light, cigarette smoke curling, sense of desperate urgency and time pressure. Muted greens, grays, warm orange highlights from the lamps. Comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes

panels.text: Across three countries, engineers and mathematicians raced to build machines that could think faster than people. They did not always know about each other's work. Different technologies, different designs — but they all converged on the same principle Turing had described: a machine that manipulates symbols according to rules.

panels.prompt: A vast 1940s computing room seen from a low angle, rows of enormous black metal cabinets stretching into the distance, thousands of blinking lights and tangled cables, two small human figures dwarfed by the machinery, orange-warm glow from vacuum tubes illuminating the scene, dramatic shadows and scale. The machines are enormous, fragile-looking, and awe-inspiring. Comic book style, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes, orange accent lighting

panels.text: The machines they built were enormous, fragile, expensive, and revolutionary. They filled entire rooms. They consumed enough electricity to power small neighborhoods. They broke down constantly. And they changed everything.

panels.text: The first person to build a programmable computer wasn't British or American. He was a German engineer, working alone, in his parents' apartment. And almost nobody noticed.
